notes.meaning: Baasha, the king of the northern kingdom of Israel, moved south and fortified the town of Ramah. This town was only five miles north of Jerusalem, sitting right on the main trade and travel road. By building a fortress here, Baasha set up a blockade to stop anyone from traveling into or out of Asa's kingdom of Judah.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The thirty-sixth year mentioned here seems to conflict with 1 Kings, where Baasha died earlier; many scholars explain this as an ancient copyist error, while others believe the years were counted from the split of the two kingdoms.

notes.meaning: Instead of turning to God for help, Asa took silver and gold from both the Lord's temple and his own palace. He sent these treasures as a bribe to Ben-hadad, the king of Aram, who ruled from Damascus. Asa used sacred gifts dedicated to God to buy the political favor of a pagan ruler.

Asa asked Ben-hadad to make a military peace treaty with him, just as their fathers had done in the past. He urged the Syrian king to break his existing alliance with Baasha so that Israel would leave Judah alone. Asa placed his confidence in human bargaining and payments rather than in the protection of the Lord.

Ben-hadad accepted Asa's bribe and sent his army commanders to attack the northern cities of Israel. The Syrian forces captured Ijon, Dan, Abel-maim, and all the storehouses in the region of Naphtali. This sudden invasion created an emergency on Israel's northern border that Baasha could not ignore.

When Baasha heard that Syria had invaded his northern territory, he immediately stopped building at Ramah and retreated. From a human viewpoint, Asa's political plan had worked perfectly and removed the immediate danger. However, apparent success in worldly terms does not mean an action is pleasing to God.

Asa gathered all the men of Judah to carry off the stones and timber that Baasha had left behind at Ramah. Asa used these captured materials to fortify the nearby border towns of Geba and Mizpah. He turned the enemy's building supplies into Judah's own defensive strongholds.

A prophet named Hanani came to Asa with a message of rebuke from God. He told the king that because he leaned on the king of Aram instead of the Lord, Aram's army had slipped out of his grasp. God had planned to give Asa a total victory over both Israel and Syria, but Asa's lack of faith threw that blessing away.

Hanani reminded Asa of the earlier battle against the Cushites and Libyans, who had brought a massive army of a million men with chariots and horsemen. When Asa cried out in faith and relied on the Lord, God handed that giant army over to him. The prophet showed that the same God could have easily delivered Judah again if Asa had only trusted Him.

God's watchful eyes constantly scan the whole earth, looking for opportunities to pour out His strength to help anyone whose heart is fully loyal to Him. Asa had acted foolishly by trusting in silver and foreign soldiers, so God decreed that Asa would face war for the rest of his days. Leaving God out of our troubles always costs far more than we expect.

Asa became enraged at the prophet's honest words and threw Hanani into prison, locking him in painful wooden stocks. During this same time, the king also began mistreating and oppressing some of his own citizens who objected to his actions. When a believer resists God's correction, anger and cruelty quickly take root.

The rest of the events of Asa's life, from his early years of faithful reform to his troubled final days, were preserved in the royal records of Judah and Israel. The writer directs readers to the standard historical archives of the kings for the complete account of his reign.

Near the end of his reign, Asa developed a severe and painful disease in his feet. Even when the illness grew worse, he refused to pray and seek the Lord, placing all his hopes in human physicians instead. His sin was not in taking medicine, but in trusting human doctors while shutting God completely out of his healing.

Asa died in the forty-first year of his reign and was laid to rest with his ancestors. After four decades on the throne, his long and mostly upright rule came to a sad and painful finish. His life stands as a sobering reminder that starting well is not enough; we must finish well too.

The people buried Asa in the family tomb he had cut into the rock in Jerusalem. They laid his body on a couch covered with fragrant perfumes and blended spices, and they lit a huge memorial fire of incense in his honor. Even though he had stumbled in his later years, Judah still remembered his many years of good service and gave him an honorable royal farewell.
